extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant and advanced general readers interested in theology/teleology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates philosophical criteria for when claims about God, freedom, and immortality count as knowledge, opinion, or faith; contrasts ontological, physico-teleological, and moral proofs and their limits for theology and religion. Useful for assessing the adequacy of different kinds of philosophical/theological proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between objects of faith and objects of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects of history and geography (and generally those knowable by our cognitive faculties) belong to things of fact; only objects of pure Reason can be things of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists that what may be believed on the path of historical faith must be separable from what is knowable as fact; only Ideas (concepts of objective reality which we cannot be theoretically certain of) can properly be matters of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Ideas as grounds for moral faith
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest final purpose (an Idea) has objective reality for us in a practical reference and is therefore a thing of faith rather than theoretical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such reality cannot be furnished theoretically, belief in these Ideas (e.g., God, Immortality, final purpose) is a 'moral faith' — justified not by speculative proofs but by their role as conditions for the moral use of Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith defined as moral habitus (not act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith (as habitus) is the moral attitude of Reason toward belief in that which is unattainable by theoretical cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith is a constant principle to assume as true what must be presupposed as a condition of the highest moral final purpose; it is a free belief grounded in Reason with adequacy for its practical design, not a theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief must be grounded on facts to be non-groundless
rubrics_metrics.description: All belief must be grounded upon facts; belief derived therefrom can be either knowledge for theoretical cognition or merely faith for practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts belong either to the natural concept (objects of sense, empirical or a priori metaphysical) or to the concept of freedom (which establishes itself through causality of Reason in certain effects). Absent such grounding, belief is groundless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and character of the ontological/metaphysico-cosmological proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontological proofs infer necessary existence from the concept of the 'Being the most real of all'; metaphysico-cosmological proofs infer predicates of an original Being from the necessity of some being somewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant notes sophistry in both arguments and argues that even if technically defensible they cannot persuade ordinary understanding or pass from scholastic dialectic into the world of sound understanding; they fail to give determinate, experiential content suitable for theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical (physico-) teleological proof is insufficient for a determinate God
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences from the purposes of nature indicate an intelligent World-Cause but do not yield a determinate concept of God or the unique, all-perfect Being required for theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical teleology may make us think of a supreme Understanding, but cannot establish Omnipotence, Omniscience, or uniqueness; at best it yields the opinion or hypothesis most conformable to our Reason, not a thing of faith sufficient for religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teleology supplies the practical ground for belief in God
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of freedom and the moral law gives a moral ground of proof that counts the Being of God as a thing of faith for practical pure Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Teleology leads to a determinate concept of the supreme Cause (possessing attributes like Omniscience and Omnipotence insofar as required by moral final purpose) and thus furnishes the conviction necessary for theology and religion, although only in a practical (not theoretical) sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of physico-teleology as propaedeutic to moral proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical teleology's merit is to guide Reason by way of purposes toward the idea of an intelligent Author, making Reason more susceptible to the moral proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if physical teleology cannot by itself establish theology, it can 'lead the mind' through observed purposiveness and thus indirectly prepare acceptance of the moral argument; it mingles unnoticed with the moral ground of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology's purpose is subjective (for religion) not extension of natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology is not needed to extend or correct our cognition of nature; it is required subjectively for Religion, i.e., the practical or moral use of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a theological concept justified by moral grounds suffices for the moral destination of belief even if it does not produce theoretical knowledge of the divine nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of determinacy for theological concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A theological concept must be determinate enough to serve the final purpose of theology (i.e., to ground religion and duties); indeterminate empirical inferences cannot provide this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a determinate concept (totality of perfections compatible with intelligence), we cannot infer a unique intelligent original Being suitable for theology; arbitrary additions to secure determinacy mean the concept is assumed, not proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of applying categories (e.g., causality) to supersensible beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories like causality can cognize objects of sense but cannot determine the concept of a supersensible Being (God) when applied theoretically, because predicates that find their object only in the world of sense leave the supersensible concept empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may 'think' a supersensible Being by analogy (e.g., an Understanding as Cause) for practical use, but one must not claim to cognize or ascribe those predicates theoretically to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Ethical (practical) theology vs theoretical theological physic
rubrics_metrics.description: An Ethical Theology (grounded on moral law) is possible and relevant for morality's final design; a Theological Physic (laws of nature as ordinances of a Highest Will) is impossible as a branch of practical reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morality can subsist without theology as rule, but to secure the final design and our orientation toward that design we need the practical postulates that Ethical Theology supplies; doctrines not given by pure practical Reason are not moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral faith vs dogmatic unbelief and doubtful faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Dogmatic unbelief (denying validity to rational Ideas because there is no theoretical ground) cannot coexist with a moral maxim; doubtful faith (absence of theoretical conviction) can coexist with moral commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be incredulous means clinging to maxims and not believing testimony in general; unbelieving judges dogmatically. A moral attitude substitutes paramount practical belief for lack of theoretical conviction, enabling action despite speculative doubts.
